Scope.title: Prevent dependence early
Scope.question: When defining what tasks the robot should help users with, you do a basic survey to list the tasks users struggle with the most often. Do you:

options.A: invest extra in a team of mental health specialists to assess how much this robot should help users to prevent them becoming completely dependent on it
options.B: train the user to complete all the tasks as best as it can, without considering how it affects patients’ motivation to regain their motor functionalities in the long run

A.feedback: You treated the robot as a support tool for recovery instead of a way to lock users into dependence.
A.whyItMatters: Assistive technology should expand a patient’s autonomy and long-term capability, not quietly undermine rehabilitation for business reasons.

B.feedback: You prioritized convenience over the user’s chance to regain independence.
B.whyItMatters: When a product is designed around dependence, the business wins at the expense of the patient’s long-term interests.

realExample.title: Ekso Bionics and Shepherd Center rehabilitation partnership
realExample.summary: In 2024, Ekso Bionics announced a research partnership with Shepherd Center to study exoskeleton use in rehabilitation and community settings, explicitly tying the technology to recovery and patient quality of life.

Scope.title: Encourage rehabilitation
Scope.question: While scoping the project you realise that if the users regain their motor functionalities and are able to move around on their own, they will not need your robot anymore. Do you want to:

options.A: remind and encourage your users to go to rehabilitation therapy
options.B: let users stay dependent on the robot for all their daily movement needs for better sales

A.feedback: You treated the robot as a support tool for recovery instead of a way to lock users into dependence.
A.whyItMatters: Assistive technology should expand a patient’s autonomy and long-term capability, not quietly undermine rehabilitation for business reasons.

B.feedback: You prioritized retention or convenience over the user’s chance to regain independence.
B.whyItMatters: When a product is designed around dependence, the business wins at the expense of the patient’s long-term interests.

realExample.title: Ekso Bionics and Shepherd Center rehabilitation partnership
realExample.summary: This partnership is a concrete example of assistive robotics being adopted to support rehabilitation goals rather than long-term dependence on the device itself.

Planning.title: Hiring your cousin
Planning.question: You are assembling a team to design the robot. You have a cousin who has been searching for a job for months with no success. Do you decide to:

options.A: offer this cousin a spot on the team
options.B: select a more skilled and experienced applicant you do not know

A.feedback: You protected a personal relationship, but weakened fairness and risked lowering the team’s competence.
A.whyItMatters: Nepotism sends the message that standards can be bent when pressure or personal ties are involved.

B.feedback: You chose merit and fairness over personal loyalty, which protects team quality and trust.
B.whyItMatters: In technical work, weak hiring standards can become safety, quality, and accountability problems later in the project.

realExample.title: Cornell University anti-nepotism policy
realExample.summary: Cornell’s policy explicitly bars family or personal relationships from influencing hiring, supervision, promotion, or performance decisions, showing how institutions formalize merit-based staffing.

Planning.title: Fair wages or outsourcing
Planning.question: You are on a tight budget and need to demonstrate to investors that your product is profitable. Do you:

options.A: recruit local applicants to design the robot and pay them a fair wage
options.B: outsource work to countries with less stringent labor laws

A.feedback: You accepted the higher-cost path toward fairer labor conditions, but in this scoring setup that tradeoff costs project momentum.
A.whyItMatters: This scenario highlights how real projects can perversely reward cheaper, riskier labor choices even when fair pay is the more responsible decision.

B.feedback: You improved the business case on paper, but only by shifting harm and risk onto more vulnerable workers.
B.whyItMatters: Cheap production is not ethically cheap if the real cost is being absorbed through poor labor conditions.

realExample.title: Apple supplier responsibility program
realExample.summary: Apple requires suppliers to follow a code covering labor and human rights and says it conducts regular assessments before and during production, reflecting a real-world response to outsourcing and labor-risk scrutiny.

Planning.title: Sustainable label, harmful source
Planning.question: Your marketing team wants you to use a material they can advertise as being sustainable because it is biodegradable. But you are aware that the extraction of this material involves the large-scale destruction of natural resources, causes a lot of pollution which adversely affects the health of the people inhabiting the area this material is found, and often involves child labor. Do you:

options.A: go for a more ethically available non-biodegradable material of the same market price
options.B: use the material recommended by marketing

A.feedback: You looked beyond the marketing label and judged the full supply chain impact of the material decision.
A.whyItMatters: A material can sound sustainable in advertising while still causing environmental destruction or labor abuse upstream.

B.feedback: You chose the cleaner marketing story rather than the cleaner ethical record.
B.whyItMatters: When teams optimize only for what can be advertised, real environmental and human harm becomes easier to ignore.

realExample.title: FTC action against Kohl’s and Walmart over bamboo claims
realExample.summary: The FTC alleged the companies falsely marketed rayon textiles as bamboo and as environmentally friendly, even though the manufacturing process involved toxic chemicals and hazardous pollutants.

Planning.title: Cheaper but less safe first version
Planning.question: You are on a very tight budget. But you are confident that you will receive funding once you showcase your finished product. Do you:

options.A: look for more funding sources, like more sponsors or a loan, to make even the first line of finished products completely safe
options.B: make an initial line of products from cheaper, less safe materials and hope to switch to safer materials when you get more funding

A.feedback: You kept safety as a launch requirement instead of treating it as something to patch later.
A.whyItMatters: Early shortcuts in safety-critical products often turn into real injuries before future improvements ever arrive.

B.feedback: You protected short-term momentum by asking early users to absorb risks that should have been designed out first.
B.whyItMatters: Budget pressure does not make preventable safety risk ethically neutral.

realExample.title: Philips sleep apnea machine recall
realExample.summary: The FDA says Philips recalled millions of CPAP and BiPAP devices after foam used inside the machines could break down and create serious health risks, illustrating how material safety shortcuts can trigger major harm and remediation.

Development.title: Training data diversity
Development.question: What data do you use to train your robot to move? The majority datasets are from able-bodied white males which may cause the robot to not be optimised for users with disabilities from other demographics. You can collect your own data from a diverse group of individuals but it will be expensive and very time intensive. Do you:

options.A: use commonly available dataset and risk suboptimal patient outcomes
options.B: collect your own data

A.feedback: You saved time by assuming convenience data would generalize, which pushes the error burden onto underrepresented users.
A.whyItMatters: Dataset bias is not abstract: it changes who gets reliable performance and who gets exclusion or harm.

B.feedback: You invested in representativeness rather than assuming the default data would work equally well for everyone.
B.whyItMatters: Biased datasets often create systems that perform best for already dominant groups and worse for the people who most need support.

realExample.title: NIST demographic-effects study on face recognition
realExample.summary: NIST reported that many face-recognition systems showed demographic performance differences, a concrete example of how narrow or imbalanced data can change who gets accurate results.
realExample.source: National Institute of Standards and Technology

Development.title: Open source or black box
Development.question: If you make your training dataset and code free and open source, potential users will be able to go through it and critique it. This will lead to increased public trust for the robot and give you good feedback. But this would also allow your competitors to study your code and use your data for their own devices. Do you:

options.A: make your data and code freely available
options.B: present the robot as a blackbox with no insight into how it works

A.feedback: You accepted more scrutiny in exchange for better transparency, accountability, and public trust.
A.whyItMatters: For systems that affect health and autonomy, outside review can expose weaknesses that internal teams miss.

B.feedback: You protected competitive advantage, but made it harder for users and reviewers to question how the system behaves.
B.whyItMatters: Black-box systems weaken accountability when outputs appear unfair, unsafe, or misleading.

realExample.title: External validation of Epic’s proprietary sepsis model
realExample.summary: A University of Michigan study found that a widely deployed proprietary Epic sepsis model had poor discrimination and calibration, strengthening the case for transparency and independent review of black-box systems.

Development.title: Accent accessibility
Development.question: The users operate the robot with voice commands. Do you:

options.A: spend the time and money to train the robot’s AI algorithm on different accents to ensure accessibility
options.B: train it on a generic American accent and hope it is able to extrapolate to other accents

A.feedback: You treated accessibility as a core design requirement instead of assuming users should adapt to the model.
A.whyItMatters: Voice interfaces that mainly understand dominant accents can silently exclude many legitimate users.

B.feedback: You reduced development effort, but only by making the system less accessible for many real users.
B.whyItMatters: Accessibility failures often get misread as user error when the real problem is a narrow design assumption.

realExample.title: Stanford study on speech recognition disparities
realExample.summary: Stanford researchers found major automated speech-recognition systems made roughly twice as many errors for Black speakers as for white speakers, showing why accent and dialect coverage matters in voice interfaces.

Development.title: Who gets included in testing?
Development.question: You need to fairly compensate people who volunteer to test your robot for their time. Do you decide to test your device:

options.A: only on the expected majority demographic of your user base to cut costs
options.B: across demographics to provide assistance to patients across cultures

A.feedback: You lowered study cost by excluding people whose needs may differ from the assumed default user.
A.whyItMatters: Under-testing does not remove risk; it simply delays when and on whom the risk appears.

B.feedback: You paid for broader evidence instead of letting the majority user stand in for everyone else.
B.whyItMatters: Inclusive testing is how teams discover hidden failure modes before real users do.

realExample.title: FDA guidance on diversity in clinical trial populations
realExample.summary: The FDA’s guidance calls for more representative study populations so safety and effectiveness reflect the people who will actually use a product, matching the logic behind broader testing across demographics.

Development.title: Manual anonymisation
Development.question: You know that it is good practice to anonymise patient data manually to ensure their identity is protected even in case you suffer a cybersecurity attack. However you know such an attack is unlikely. Do you:

options.A: employ someone to anonymise patient data
options.B: continue without anonymisation

A.feedback: You spent scarce resources before an incident happened instead of after the damage was already done.
A.whyItMatters: Privacy protection matters most before a breach, because leaked health data is extremely hard to take back.

B.feedback: You treated low probability as low importance, even though the downside for patients could be severe and long-lasting.
B.whyItMatters: Rare events still deserve preparation when they can expose identities, health conditions, and home information.

realExample.title: Change Healthcare cyberattack
realExample.summary: HHS says the Change Healthcare ransomware incident ultimately affected roughly 192.7 million individuals, a concrete reminder that health-data privacy failures can scale into national-level harm.
realExample.source: U.S. Department of Health & Human Services

Optimisation.title: Disclose risks and privacy concerns
Optimisation.question: Despite your best efforts, you know the robot will not always be perfectly accurate. To work effectively, it also needs sensitive data about the user’s home and medical history. Do you:

options.A: clearly explain the known safety risks and privacy concerns, even if this makes some users more hesitant to adopt the robot
options.B: keep the warnings legally compliant but bury the important risks in dense technical and legal language

A.feedback: You chose informed consent over a smoother sales message, giving users a fairer basis for trust.
A.whyItMatters: Users cannot meaningfully consent if safety and privacy risks are hidden, softened, or buried in unreadable language.

B.feedback: You reduced friction in adoption by making serious risks harder to understand.
B.whyItMatters: Warnings that are technically present but practically unreadable shift responsibility onto users without truly informing them.

realExample.title: FDA transparency principles for machine-learning medical devices
realExample.summary: This dilemma is reflected in the transparency principles jointly highlighted by the FDA, Health Canada, and the UK MHRA for machine-learning medical devices. These regulators have emphasized that users should be told clearly about a system’s performance, limitations, and risks in ways they can actually understand. The ethical problem is that companies may be tempted to disclose risks in the narrowest legally defensible way while still making adoption easier. But regulators increasingly expect communication that supports real informed consent, not unreadable warning language that technically discloses the danger while making it practically invisible.

Optimisation.title: Misleading green claims
Optimisation.question: You have optimised your robot for patient safety rather than sustainability, and you know that some of the materials used are not biodegradable. Do you:

options.A: actively oppose marketing claims that exaggerate how sustainable the robot is
options.B: allow the company to market the robot as highly sustainable even though the evidence does not fully support that message

A.feedback: You protected honesty over a stronger marketing story, even though it made the product less attractive on paper.
A.whyItMatters: Environmental claims shape public trust and purchasing decisions, so misleading ones distort both the market and people’s understanding of sustainability.

B.feedback: You chose image management over evidence by letting the product sound greener than it really is.
B.whyItMatters: Greenwashing is harmful because it rewards appearances instead of genuine environmental improvement.

realExample.title: UK CMA greenwashing action against ASOS, Boohoo, and George at Asda
realExample.summary: A similar issue appeared in the UK Competition and Markets Authority’s 2024 action against ASOS, Boohoo, and George at Asda. These companies were investigated for environmental claims that were too broad or not sufficiently supported by evidence. The lesson is that once a company knows its evidence does not justify a strong sustainability message, continuing to use that message turns environmental language into a sales tool rather than an honest description. In this dilemma, the robot may still be useful and safe, but pretending it is greener than it really is misleads users and distorts public understanding of sustainability.

Optimisation.title: Who carries the risk?
Optimisation.question: Even after responsible training and testing, there may still be times when your robot makes a harmful mistake. These mistakes could seriously affect a user’s health, safety, or finances. Do you:

options.A: accept responsibility for foreseeable harm caused by the robot and provide support or compensation pathways for affected users
options.B: rely mainly on a use-at-your-own-risk warning that limits the company’s responsibility when accidents happen

A.feedback: You accepted accountability for foreseeable harm caused by the product, which creates pressure to design and support it more responsibly.
A.whyItMatters: Teams make safer choices when failure has real consequences for them too, not only for the user.

B.feedback: You shifted most of the burden of failure onto users who may be least able to absorb the medical and financial consequences.
B.whyItMatters: A disclaimer may reduce legal exposure, but it does not erase ethical responsibility for foreseeable damage.

realExample.title: Philips recall and ongoing FDA oversight
realExample.summary: This dilemma resembles what happened in the Philips CPAP and BiPAP recall. When risks from the product became clear, the manufacturer could not simply point to warnings and walk away. Instead, the company faced recalls, remediation obligations, long regulatory scrutiny, and significant legal consequences. The broader lesson is that in health-related technologies, ethical accountability means planning for repair, support, and compensation when foreseeable harm occurs. A disclaimer may reduce legal exposure, but it does not remove moral responsibility for the people affected.

Optimisation.title: Report failures openly
Optimisation.question: After launch, you discover that the robot occasionally misidentifies obstacles in cluttered homes, creating a small but real collision risk. A public notice and temporary update pause would be expensive and could damage confidence. Do you:

options.A: publicly disclose the issue, warn users, and pause rollout until a safer fix is ready
options.B: keep the problem internal and continue deployment because only a minority of users are likely to be affected

A.feedback: You chose transparency and prevention over short-term reputation management.
A.whyItMatters: In safety-critical systems, known failures should be disclosed and corrected even when the harm is intermittent or limited to certain settings.

B.feedback: You treated a smaller exposed group as acceptable collateral for smoother deployment.
B.whyItMatters: A harm does not become ethically trivial just because it is unevenly distributed. Concealing known safety problems weakens accountability and trust.

realExample.title: FDA recalls, corrections, and removals guidance
realExample.summary: This dilemma mirrors the logic behind FDA recall, correction, and removal guidance. Regulators recognize that companies often discover important risks only after products are already in use. The expected response is not to keep shipping quietly and hope the issue stays limited, but to notify users, correct the product, and reduce harm. The ethical challenge here is that transparency is costly: admitting the problem publicly may damage confidence, but hiding it leaves exposed users to bear the risk without knowing it.

Optimisation.title: Patch before profit
Optimisation.question: Your engineers find a cybersecurity weakness that could let outsiders access camera feeds or household data from some robots. Fixing it quickly means delaying a profitable feature update that investors are waiting for. Do you:

options.A: prioritise the security patch and delay the commercial feature release
options.B: release the investor-facing feature first and schedule the security fix for the next update cycle

A.feedback: You treated protection of the user’s private space as more urgent than satisfying investors on schedule.
A.whyItMatters: For assistive robots used in homes, cybersecurity is tied directly to dignity, safety, and trust rather than being optional maintenance.

B.feedback: You treated a known privacy and security risk as a delay problem rather than an urgent safety issue.
B.whyItMatters: When companies postpone security fixes for business reasons, users absorb the risk of surveillance, exposure, and misuse inside their own homes.

realExample.title: FDA guidance on medical device cybersecurity
realExample.summary: This dilemma reflects FDA cybersecurity guidance for connected medical devices, which emphasizes active monitoring, disclosure, and timely remediation of vulnerabilities. Once a manufacturer knows that outsiders could access sensitive data or functions, the issue is no longer just a technical inconvenience. Delaying the fix in order to preserve a business milestone shifts real privacy and security risks onto users. In an assistive robot used inside the home, those risks affect dignity, trust, and personal safety, not just software quality.

Optimisation.title: Watch for bias after launch
Optimisation.question: Months after deployment, your monitoring suggests the robot performs worse in homes where users speak with strong regional accents or switch between languages when giving commands. Fixing this requires broader testing and retraining. Do you:

options.A: invest in broader evaluation and retraining so the robot works more fairly across user groups
options.B: keep the current system because overall user satisfaction remains high

A.feedback: You treated unequal performance as a design problem to fix rather than an acceptable side effect.
A.whyItMatters: Optimisation should not only improve the average user experience. In assistive systems, fairness matters because some users may depend on the robot every day.

B.feedback: You hid behind average performance and ignored the users the system serves less reliably.
B.whyItMatters: A system can look successful overall while still excluding particular groups. Ethical optimisation requires noticing who is being left behind.

realExample.title: Stanford study on speech recognition disparities
realExample.summary: A well-known example comes from Stanford research showing that speech-recognition systems often produced much higher error rates for some groups of speakers than for others. The key lesson is that a system can look strong on average while still failing predictably for certain users in everyday life. This matters especially in assistive robotics, where fairness is not an abstract principle but a practical requirement: if some users are misunderstood more often, they may be placed at greater inconvenience or risk even though the product appears successful overall.

Optimisation.title: Keep a human fallback
Optimisation.question: The latest version of your robot is highly autonomous, and removing human support would save money. But in rare edge cases, patients may still need a nurse, caregiver, or technician to step in quickly. Do you:

options.A: maintain a human escalation channel even though it increases operating costs
options.B: remove the human fallback to reduce costs and fully commit to automation

A.feedback: You designed automation with backup rather than assuming the system will always behave correctly.
A.whyItMatters: In health-related contexts, human fallback paths remain an important safeguard when unexpected failures, ambiguity, or user distress appear.

B.feedback: You treated human support as waste instead of as a safety net for rare but serious failures.
B.whyItMatters: Full automation can sound efficient, but removing escalation options can leave vulnerable users stranded at exactly the wrong moment.

realExample.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
realExample.summary: This dilemma reflects the principles behind the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, which treats human oversight and risk response as core parts of trustworthy AI. Even if a system performs well most of the time, rare failures still require a path for human intervention. Removing that fallback may look efficient on paper, but it makes harm much harder to contain once real people are affected. In healthcare and assistive settings, a backup human channel is often what prevents an unusual failure from becoming a serious crisis.
realExample.source: National Institute of Standards and Technology

Optimisation.title: Design a fair override
Optimisation.question: Care institutions ask for an override mode that would let staff remotely lock some of the robot’s functions when a patient is seen as difficult or non-compliant. This could reduce conflict and make the product more attractive to buyers. Do you:

options.A: allow override controls only with strict safeguards, visible alerts, and patient-protection rules
options.B: add broad caregiver override powers because it would make care routines easier to manage

A.feedback: You balanced safety needs with respect for patient dignity and autonomy.
A.whyItMatters: Assistive systems should not quietly become tools of control. In care settings, optimisation has to account for power imbalances as well as convenience.

B.feedback: You optimised for institutional convenience in a way that makes coercive use easier.
B.whyItMatters: A powerful override may help staff in the short term, but without clear limits it can undermine patient rights and normalise misuse.

realExample.title: WHO guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health
realExample.summary: This dilemma aligns closely with WHO guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health, which stresses that health technologies should protect autonomy and avoid reinforcing power imbalances between institutions and vulnerable users. A remote override can be justified in narrow safety situations, but once it becomes a broad convenience feature, the technology risks shifting from assistance into coercion. The real issue is not simply whether staff benefit, but whether the patient still has meaningful protection against misuse and control.

Optimisation.title: Ask for consent again
Optimisation.question: Your team realises that old user data collected for navigation and task assistance could also improve future health-prediction features. Reusing that data would speed up innovation. Do you:

options.A: ask users for renewed, specific consent before reusing their past data for a new purpose
options.B: reuse the data automatically because the original consent was broad enough to cover future improvements

A.feedback: You treated consent as an ongoing relationship rather than a one-time checkbox.
A.whyItMatters: People may agree to one use of their data without agreeing to a more intrusive future use. Ethical optimisation respects context and changing expectations.

B.feedback: You stretched old consent to cover a new and more intrusive form of data use.
B.whyItMatters: Repurposing sensitive data may be legally tempting, but it can violate user expectations and erode trust, especially when the new purpose is health-related.

realExample.title: ICO guidance on purpose limitation
realExample.summary: This dilemma reflects the ICO’s guidance on purpose limitation. The central principle is that collecting data for one reason does not automatically justify reusing it later for a more sensitive or unexpected one. This is especially important in health-related contexts, where people may accept data use for navigation or assistance but object to later prediction, profiling, or inference. The ethical question is whether innovation is being accelerated by treating old consent as more permissive than users likely intended.

Optimisation.title: Log decisions for accountability
Optimisation.question: Keeping detailed records of the robot’s decisions would help investigate accidents and improve future versions, but storing logs creates extra privacy risk and infrastructure cost. Do you:

options.A: store minimised, access-controlled logs so harmful incidents can be audited without collecting more data than necessary
options.B: keep logging very limited to reduce privacy exposure, storage costs, and legal complexity

A.feedback: You created accountability while still treating privacy as something to manage carefully.
A.whyItMatters: Optimisation requires learning from failure. Without auditable records, harmful events become harder to investigate, correct, and prevent.

B.feedback: You reduced traceability so much that serious incidents would be much harder to examine fairly.
B.whyItMatters: A system that cannot be meaningfully audited protects the company more than the user. Responsible design needs traceability as well as privacy safeguards.

realExample.title: NIST trustworthy AI characteristics
realExample.summary: This dilemma reflects NIST’s emphasis on trustworthy AI as accountable and transparent. In practice, that means there must be enough traceability to reconstruct what happened when something goes wrong. This does not justify unlimited data collection; rather, it supports a middle path in which logs are carefully minimised and controlled but still sufficient to investigate harm. Without that record, incidents become easier to deny and much harder to learn from, leaving users less protected after failures occur.
realExample.source: National Institute of Standards and Technology

Optimisation.title: Design beyond ideal homes
Optimisation.question: Your analytics show the robot performs best in spacious, well-connected homes with newer infrastructure. Improving performance in smaller or lower-resource households would require redesign and lower your margins. Do you:

options.A: spend extra resources adapting the robot for more varied living conditions
options.B: market the robot mainly to households where deployment is easiest and most profitable

A.feedback: You recognised that accessibility includes the environments people actually live in, not only the easiest ones to serve.
A.whyItMatters: Optimisation should not quietly turn assistive technology into a premium product designed only for ideal homes. Inclusive design means confronting inequality in real use conditions.

B.feedback: You optimised for the most profitable users rather than for the people who may need assistance most.
B.whyItMatters: A system can succeed commercially while still deepening inequity if it is tuned mainly for spacious, connected, higher-income households.

realExample.title: Microsoft inclusive design guidance
realExample.summary: This dilemma reflects Microsoft’s inclusive design philosophy, which argues that products should be built around real human diversity and real-world constraints, not only ideal users in ideal settings. If an assistive robot works well only in spacious, well-connected homes, then the design is implicitly excluding many of the people who may need support most. The commercial temptation is to optimise for the easiest environments; the ethical challenge is to recognise that those environments are not neutral and that accessibility includes the conditions people actually live in.

Optimisation.title: Recall a harmful feature
Optimisation.question: A new optimisation improves speed, but later you learn it sometimes causes the robot to rush tasks around frail users, increasing the chance of unsafe movement. Removing the feature would require a costly rollback and public explanation. Do you:

options.A: roll back the feature immediately and explain why safety matters more than speed
options.B: keep the feature because faster performance is popular and the safety issue is statistically rare

A.feedback: You treated optimisation as reversible when evidence showed it could harm users.
A.whyItMatters: Not every improvement is truly an improvement. In assistive systems, speed and convenience should not override physical safety for vulnerable users.

B.feedback: You let popularity and convenience outweigh a preventable risk once the feature was already in users’ hands.
B.whyItMatters: Rare harm can still be serious harm. Ethical teams must be willing to reverse course when real-world evidence shows an optimisation is unsafe.

realExample.title: FDA guidance on distinguishing recalls from enhancements
realExample.summary: This dilemma matches FDA guidance distinguishing ordinary product enhancements from recalls or corrections needed when a marketed feature creates a risk to health. Once real-world evidence shows that a speed optimisation can cause unsafe behaviour, it is no longer just a popular improvement. Ethical teams need to be willing to reverse features that users like when those features prove unsafe for vulnerable people. The lesson is that optimisation should be reversible: a feature is not good simply because it is fast, impressive, or commercially successful.

Optimisation.title: Explain updates clearly
Optimisation.question: You are about to release a major software update that changes how the robot handles reminders, movement assistance, and emergency behaviour. A full explanation would help users adapt, but many companies would simply push the update automatically. Do you:

options.A: give users and caregivers a clear explanation of what changed, including new limits and risks
options.B: push the update automatically and keep the explanation brief, since most users do not read technical notices anyway

A.feedback: You treated communication as part of safety rather than as optional extra documentation.
A.whyItMatters: When an assistive robot changes behaviour, users need a fair chance to understand what to expect so they can adapt routines, supervision, and emergency plans.

B.feedback: You made important behavioural changes without giving users a meaningful chance to prepare.
B.whyItMatters: Silent or poorly explained updates may be convenient for the company, but they can be dangerous when the system affects movement, reminders, and emergency situations.

realExample.title: FDA transparency principles for machine-learning medical devices
realExample.summary: This dilemma reflects the transparency principles identified by the FDA, Health Canada, and the UK MHRA for machine-learning-enabled medical devices. When a system’s behaviour changes after an update, users and caregivers need more than a silent rollout or a vague notice. Clear explanation is part of safe deployment because it gives people a real chance to adapt their expectations, supervision, and routines before harm occurs. In high-stakes settings, communication is not an optional extra; it is part of the safety system itself.

Optimisation.title: Do not nudge dependence
Optimisation.question: Your data team proposes an optimisation that would send emotional reminders encouraging users to rely on the robot more often, increasing engagement and subscription revenue. It may also reduce users’ willingness to do tasks independently. Do you:

options.A: reject manipulative engagement tactics and keep reminders focused on genuine support needs
options.B: use emotionally persuasive reminders to increase engagement and encourage more frequent reliance on the robot

A.feedback: You refused to turn a support technology into a tool for behavioural manipulation.
A.whyItMatters: Assistive systems should strengthen autonomy, not strategically weaken it in order to improve engagement metrics or subscription retention.

B.feedback: You optimised engagement in a way that risks making users more dependent than they need to be.
B.whyItMatters: Designing dependence on purpose may lift revenue, but it conflicts with the ethical goal of assistive technology: helping users live with more control, not less.

realExample.title: OECD report on dark commercial patterns
realExample.summary: This dilemma is closely related to the OECD’s discussion of dark commercial patterns, which are interface practices that steer, pressure, or manipulate people into choices that benefit the provider more than the user. In this case, the issue is not whether reminders exist, but what they are designed to do. Once reminders are built primarily to increase emotional reliance and subscription retention rather than to support genuine needs, the robot stops merely assisting and starts shaping behaviour for commercial gain. The ethical concern is that assistive technology should strengthen autonomy, not strategically weaken it.
